newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto gives up finance post in economic shake-up.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto gives up finance post in economic shake-up.

text.p: Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto gave up the finance portfolio she has held for three years and named her privatisation chief to the post on Monday, a government spokesman said.
He said Privatisation Minister Syed Naveed Qamar, 41, a Bhutto loyalist, had been appointed as Minister for Finance and Economic Affairs and was also keeping his old portfolio.

Bhutto had been her own finance minister since taking power in October 1993, appointing Makhdoom Shahabuddin as State Minister for Finance. However, the ministry was actually run by Bhutto's adviser for finance and economic affairs V.A. Jafarey.
Critics had argued that Bhutto lacked the expertise to run the finance ministry herself and should appoint a new economic team to try to restore Pakistan's battered international image.
The spokesman said that Jafarey, widely reported to have offered his resignation last week, had applied for three months' leave, but Bhutto allowed him only one month.
He said he had no information on whether Shahabuddin would retain his present position or get a new portfolio.

Another official said Moeen Afzal, additional secretary at the Finance Ministry, had been promoted to secretary in place of Mian Tayyeb, known to be close to Jafarey. Tayyeb was transferred to the Ministry of Industries and Production.
State-run television said Hussain Lawai, chairman of the private Muslim Commercial Bank had been named consultant to the Finance Ministry. It did not say what his functions would be.

Qamar, a big landowner with longstanding links to Bhutto's ruling Pakistan People's Party, became privatisation minister in a cabinet expansion in July, when the privatisation commission he had headed was upgraded to a full division.
A member of the National Assembly (lower house), Qamar comes from a prominent political family in the southern province of Sindh.

He holds a master's degree in business administration from California University, a degree in management from Northrop University in the United States, and a bachelor's degree in computer science from Britain's Manchester University.
"The changes have apparently been done to improve credibility with the IMF," said an analyst at a foreign brokerage house, who asked not be named.
The analyst said it should now be clear who was responsible for economic policy-making.

Previously, several people, including Jafarey, Bhutto's special assistant for the economy Shahid Hasan Khan and State (central) Bank Governor Muhammad Yaqub, as well as Bhutto herself, seemed to wield varying degrees of influence.
The International Monetary Fund, which sent a mission to Islamabad on Saturday, is known to have shown scepticism at some of the economic data provided by Bhutto's former team.

The IMF had earlier made clear that its patience with Pakistan's repeated failures to meet agreed targets was running thin, saying that it would only send a team after a comprehensive and "credible" stabilisation package was in place.
The IMF has delayed disbursements of a $600 million standby loan provided in December 1995 and must complete a review of the standby agreement before payments can be resumed.
Pakistan needs an IMF seal of approval for its economic policies to stave off a threatened downgrade of its credit ratings and maintain access to international capital markets.
Parliamentary Affairs Minister Sher Afgan Niazi was given the additional portfolio of human rights, previously held by Iqbal Haider, who was named attorney general earlier this month.
